source: Agriculture Sector Development Project (ASDP), ADB Loan No. 2023-CAM(SF), Guide No.1: Coconut-damaging beetle and protective measures, prepared by Kampot Province Department of Agricultural Extension, 2008
text:
The guide presents Asecodes hispinarum, a small black parasitic wasp (body about 1 mm long) originally sourced from Western Samoa, as the main recommended biological control method against the coconut-damaging beetle, alongside chemical and mechanical control options.

Wasp life cycle and behavior: a single female wasp can produce roughly 30 to 160 offspring over her reproductive life (figure as printed in the source). Development inside the host beetle larva (the pupal/parasitism stage) takes about 16-18 days under suitable conditions (around 28°C), and the emerged adult wasp itself lives only about 3-5 days, during which it must find and parasitize new host larvae.

The wasp targets coconut beetle larvae specifically, attacking hosts from the 1st through 4th larval instar, with a preference for laying eggs into 4th-instar larvae. Its slender body lets it reach into the tight, folded young coconut leaflets where beetle larvae feed and hide. The wasp does not harm humans and uses the beetle larva purely as a food/development source for its own offspring, effectively killing the pest larva in the process.

Parasitism sequence as illustrated: the female wasp lays eggs (the guide notes 2 eggs) into a host beetle larva; by about day 5 the wasp's own larva is visible inside the host as a pale, clear-colored grub; by about day 7 the wasp larva has attached to and begun consuming the host from within; by about day 10 the wasp larva has darkened to a brownish color; by about day 15 it has turned dark brown to purple and is ready to pupate. Around day 17-25 (as printed; the exact end of this range is not fully legible in the source) the new adult wasp chews its way out of the dead host larva ('mummy') and emerges. A single parasitized host larva can yield approximately 30 to 60 new adult wasps.

Mass rearing: because natural wasp populations alone often cannot multiply fast enough for effective field-wide control, the guide describes controlled indoor rearing to boost wasp numbers, matching rearing conditions (temperature, humidity, food supply of host larvae) to the wasp's natural requirements, shown in the guide with photographs of shelved rearing containers and collected host larvae in a laboratory setting.
